extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of 18th-century periodical essays; general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative observations relevant to composing or understanding short, opinionated periodical essays (Spectator-style), including topical humor, social commentary, and mannered anecdote. Emphases include tasteful phrasing, character-sketch conventions, and how to present reports and epitaphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph style: diffused/pathetic vs close/contracted
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal manners of epitaph-writing: "the first being in the diffused and luxuriant, the second in the close contracted Style. The first has much of the Simple and Pathetick; the second is something Light, but Nervous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are given to illustrate each: a long, flowing, pathetic epitaph (e.g. 'Here Thomas Sapper lyes interred...' with family details and sentiment) versus a terse, witty inscription ('Here lies the Body of Daniel Saul, Spittle-fields Weaver, and that's all.'). Use the long form to elicit pathos and the short form for light, punchy effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy as indicator of profession/taste
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a close correspondence between outward appearance and inward character; physiognomy can typify intellectual and artistic dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific markers map to kinds of persons/artistic temperaments: 'a contracted Brow, a lumpish down-cast Look, a sober sedate Pace... is Logick, Metaphysicks and Mathematicks in Perfection.' Belles-lettres: 'a Saunter in the Gate... a negligent Swing... a Pinch of right and fine Barcelona between Finger and Thumb.' Grave solemn stalking Pace signals heroick poetry and politicks; an open Breast and audacious Display of the Holland Shirt is construed a tendency to the military. Use such physical detail to sketch character rapidly; the passage treats these correspondences as conventional signals an adept can read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration's force often lies in nonverbal cues
rubrics_metrics.description: In relations, 'the force of the Expression lies very often more in the Look, the Tone of Voice, or the Gesture, than the Words themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When repeating or reporting a narration, be aware that the original force may be lost or altered because nonverbal cues do not transfer through mere verbal repetition. This explains why second-hand reports often differ from originals and why a successful account sometimes depends on conveying tone and gesture as well as facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of narrators/liars (Matter-of-Fact Man; Reciters vs Embellishers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everyone who reports events can report them faithfully; certain types are unreliable. A 'Matter of Fact Man' may in practice be unable to represent what he has seen or heard. There are two sorts of liars: those with 'much Impudence and a strong Memory' (reciters) and those who add 'a good Understanding and smooth Language' (embellishers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciters repeat what they heard as literally as possible; embellishers improve the tale with invention and polish. Beware narrators who habitually amplify or smooth stories — they may invent consistency (e.g., the man who tells a lie at Charing-Cross and then tracks it through town). For writers, recognizing these types helps decide how much to trust or satirize narrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical tactic for contesting sensational reports
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical method of doubt: rather than opposing the whole report flatly, contest the single particular manner the teller fixes on and leave open the many other possibilities ('there are a hundred Ways of any thing happening, besides that it has happen'd').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rhetorical or wagering tactic, denying the teller's exact version (one of many possible ways events could have occurred) gives you greater probability of success and deflates rash narratives. This is presented both as a conversational strategy and as a method to expose overconfident narrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coffee-house etiquette / posture signals attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Good breeding requires maintaining the figure of keenest attention in a coffee-house; the 'true Posture' consists 'in leaning over a Table, with the Edge of it pressing hard upon your Stomach.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a satirical prescription for social performance: exaggeration of physical attentiveness (even to the point of discomfort) signals interest and civility. The more pain the narrator receives, the more gracious the listener's bending appears; observe such stage-managed gestures when writing scenes of public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtuous sorrow / male widowhood: equanimity as a mark of goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'a certain Equanimity in those who are good and just, which runs into their very Sorrow' — the virtuous experience sorrow that refines rather than destroys them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than recommending affectless hardness, the letter argues that true virtue produces a measured, improving sorrow (converted 'all Roughness of Temper into Meekness, Good-nature, and Complacency'). For writers depicting grief, show a sober, steadying sorrow that evidences integrity rather than theatrical excess; note the consolatory role of remembrance and modest rules of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public displays at a man's death convey character (bequests, mourning customs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funeral arrangements, bequests, and local mourning customs are presented as outward signs of a man's character and community standing ('he has bequeath'd... For Mourning, to every Man in the Parish, a great Frize-Coat, and to every Woman a black Riding-hood').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details such as charitable legacies, gifts to servants, burial location, pall-bearers, and whether a corpse was carried by tenants or accompanied by the parish reflect social virtues and produce an emotive picture. Use concrete funerary particulars to signal the deceased's values and elicit communal feeling; beware of inconsistent reports (some correspondents omit these details).
